chapter: Los Angeles 1947-48, Rock Island and bebop in New York
title: 52nd Street and New York as the big leagues
summary: If you hadn't played 52nd Street you weren't a musician; New York musicians were mostly from elsewhere.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Yeah. Uh-huh. But 52nd Street was the heart, the meat part of music, you know, in New York. If you didn't play on 52nd Street during that time you hadn't lived, you wasn't a musician. If you stayed up in Harlem, you just shouldn't have, you know, because you got lost in the shuffle and didn't anyone know anything about you if you didn't come to 52nd Street. And there were musicians in families that was born and raised in Harlem that had never been out of Harlem. I couldn't understand that. With all the freedom that they had in New York, to do things in New York that you couldn't do anywhere else. 24 hours a day something was happening. I was rest broken for two weeks at a time, for fear I was going to miss something. I'd go home and get in bed, my eyes would pop open, I'd get up and put my clothes on and I'd find some music playing somewhere. A jam session or something, you know. And if it wasn't that, I'd go to an all-night theater, you know, or an after hours spot or something. There's always something doing in New York. And I found out that the native New Yorkers were inferior musicians. Let them tell you verbally, they were the better end. But everyone there that was playing was from someplace else. Maybe from the south or from Detroit or Pittsburgh or Cleveland, you know.
New York was the place to be heard.
Yeah. New York was the -- how do you say? The big leagues.
